name: bluebox
workload: memtier_benchmark with default options against a local server on one machine (about 10% SET, 90% GET by the table's ops/sec; every GET missed), Redis started with --appendonly no --save "", Bluebox serving SET/GET/DEL/PING on port 9999.
claimed_speedup: Totals 493,346.12 ops/sec (Bluebox) vs 207,734.88 ops/sec (redis-server), about 2.4x (derived from page data); average latency 0.40524 ms vs 0.96274 ms, p99 0.46300 ms vs 1.87100 ms, p99.9 0.74300 ms vs 3.16700 ms.
compiler_and_flags: Makefile builds with ${CC} -O3 -g ${CFLAGS} src/*.c; compiler name and version not stated, Redis version and build not stated, memtier_benchmark version not stated.
hardware: Linux, AMD Ryzen 9 5950X 16-Core (README); kernel, client/server placement and core pinning not stated.
tradeoffs: Demo server for the Neco coroutine library (one coroutine per connection), not a Redis replacement: supports only SET, GET, DEL and PING, no persistence, replication, expiry, pub/sub or data structures beyond a string hashmap. Vendors neco.c (v0.3.2) and tidwall's hashmap.c (v0.8.0) under src/. No pthread use appears in src/bluebox.c, so it runs on one OS thread like default redis-server.
caveats: First-party README numbers on one run with no repetitions or variance; app-level comparison of a 4-command server against a full-featured Redis, so the gap mostly reflects how much less work Bluebox does per request, not the event-loop mechanism alone (it does not isolate Neco from Redis's epoll loop). Both tables show 0.00 hits/sec and all GETs counted as misses, so the GET path measured is the not-found path, not a value copy. Redis version, memtier version, compiler and kernel are unstated. The repo has no LICENSE file (GitHub shows no license): the vendored neco.c and hashmap.c headers say MIT-style, but Bluebox's own code is unlicensed, hence usability reference. Neco itself is catalogued; this record is the Redis comparison only. Last commit 2025-05-27, about 16 months before 2026-10-07.
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/tidwall/bluebox README (read through raw.githubusercontent.com and a github.com page fetch); src/ listing and Makefile also read.

name: Model Streamer (formerly Run:ai Model Streamer, runai-model-streamer)
baseline: Hugging Face safetensors loader (the vLLM default loader); also Tensorizer 2.9.0
workload: Time to load Meta-Llama-3-8B (15 GB, single safetensors file) into one NVIDIA A10G GPU on AWS g5.12xlarge from GP3 SSD, IO2 SSD and S3, cold start, plus time until a vLLM 0.5.5 engine is ready to serve.
claimed_speedup: Load to GPU: GP3 SSD 14.34 s (concurrency 16) vs Safetensors Loader 47.99 s, about 3.3x (derived from page data); IO2 SSD 7.53 s (concurrency 8) vs 47 s, about 6.2x (derived from page data). vLLM ready: GP3 35.08 s vs 66.13 s (about 1.9x, derived), IO2 28.28 s vs 62.69 s (about 2.2x, derived). Against Tensorizer: S3 4.88 s (concurrency 32) vs 37.36 s (16 workers), about 7.7x (derived); GP3 14.34 s vs 16.11 s; IO2 7.53 s vs 10.36 s; vLLM on S3 23.18 s vs 65.18 s (about 2.8x, derived).
hardware: AWS g5.12xlarge (4x NVIDIA A10G, one GPU used); GP3 SSD 750 GB, 16,000 IOPS, 1,000 MiB/s; IO2 SSD 500 GB, 100,000 IOPS, up to 4,000 MiB/s; S3 bucket in the same region. CPU model not stated. Software: CUDA 12.4, vLLM 0.5.5, Model Streamer 0.6.0, Tensorizer 2.9.0, Transformers 4.45.0.dev0, Accelerate 0.34.2.
stars_or_usage: 383 stars; integrated into vLLM as a model loader; pip package runai-model-streamer
tradeoffs: Python SDK over a C++ reader library (concurrent reads, optional libaio/io_uring/buffered strategies, S3, GCS and Azure backends); stays on the safetensors format, no conversion, unlike Tensorizer, which needs weights serialized to its own format. Needs libcurl and libssl; builds libstreamers3.so statically linked to libssl, libcrypto and libcurl by default. Gains depend on storage that scales with concurrency; on GP3 the win is capped by the disk's 1 GiB/s limit.
caveats: The catalogued id https://github.com/run-ai/runai-model-streamer now redirects here: the README notice says that on September 13, 2026 Run:ai Model Streamer was renamed to Model Streamer and moved from the run-ai organization to dsx-ai-factory/model-streamer, PyPI package and import names unchanged; a WebFetch of the old URL returned the new repo and the old-path README on raw.githubusercontent.com is byte-identical to the new one. Fold the old record as a duplicate with a repo_url correction. Benchmark is first-party (the project's maintainers, copyright NVIDIA in LICENSE), a results write-up without a runnable script: no benchmark code in the repo (it uses vLLM integration and Tensorizer's own recipe), CPU model and kernel not stated, so tier C. Numbers are old: Model Streamer 0.6.0 and vLLM 0.5.5 (2024 era), the repo is now past that. Baseline is the vLLM-bundled safetensors loader, not PyTorch torch.load; the safetensors time of 47.99 s on GP3 is almost the same as Model Streamer at concurrency 1 (47.56 s), so the win comes from parallel reads, not a faster single stream, and the safetensors loader gets one sequential cold read (roughly 0.3 GB/s from a disk that allows 1 GiB/s). Cold start was forced only by storage choice and, for S3, a two-minute wait; no cache drop command is named. Single run per cell, no variance. Tensorizer ran without optional hashing. Docs figures are images plus tables; only tables were read. A Microsoft Azure SDK blog (up to 6x with Azure Blob) and an NVIDIA developer blog were seen in search results but not opened (egress blocked or not needed).
found_via: seed-record pass: https://github.com/dsx-ai-factory/model-streamer README, its docs/src/benchmarks.md, and the redirect check of https://github.com/run-ai/runai-model-streamer; one WebSearch for the benchmark title confirmed the table numbers.
